Dexmedetomidine.category: Specialist advice and/or input may be required
points: Reported administration as bolus dosing, intermittent or continuous subcutaneous infusion.
Reported bioavailability of more than 80% after a single subcutaneous 10-minute infusion.
Dilute in sodium chloride 0.9%.

Famotidine.category: Specialist advice and/or input may be required
points: Not registered in Australia under the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA); only available through the Special Access Scheme (SAS).
Reported administration as bolus dosing or continuous subcutaneous infusion.
Dilute in sodium chloride 0.9% or water for injection.

Levetiracetam.category: Specialist advice and/or input may be required
points: Reported administration included infusion in 50 mL of sodium chloride 0.9% over 24 hours or intermittent infusion over 30 minutes.
There are observational reports of admixtures containing up to 1000 mg of levetiracetam diluted to at least 18 mL.

Ranitidine.category: Specialist advice and/or input may be required
points: Not registered in Australia under the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA); only available through the Special Access Scheme (SAS).
Reported administration as bolus dosing or continuous subcutaneous infusion.
Dilute in sodium chloride 0.9% or water for injection.
Known incompatibility with levomepromazine and phenobarbital.
Ranitidine should always be the last medicine added to an already diluted combination of medicines.
Intravenous administration is preferred; however continuous or intermittent subcutaneous infusions can be considered (seek specialist advice).
Dilute maximally in sodium chloride 0.9%.
Solution is alkaline — high risk of incompatibility, especially with acidic medications. Known incompatibility with metoclopramide and midazolam.
A pH-neutral or buffered formulation is commercially available internationally.
For use in a specialist setting only as it requires intermittent or continuing ECG and clinical monitoring.
Limited compatibility data and volume constraints exist.
Phenobarbital has an alkaline pH and can cause tissue necrosis when administered as a subcutaneous bolus injection.
In practice, phenobarbital can be initiated with a bolus intramuscular or intravenous injection, then via subcutaneous infusion with sodium chloride 0.9% as diluent.
Bolus subcutaneous injections up to 130 mg in 2 mL were not correlated with site reactions in one case series.
It should be given via a separate syringe driver. Dilution up to 10 times is recommended.
Seek specialist advice.
Limited safety and efficacy data exists.
Case reports of esomeprazole and omeprazole being used subcutaneously.
Reports of administering as an infusion alone.
Dilute maximally with either water for injection or sodium chloride 0.9%.
Limited safety data available; however reports of tissue necrosis.
Dexamethasone has a long half-life and bolus dosing is recommended.
Reports of use within a syringe driver to prevent infusion site reactions; however use limited due to incompatibility (seek specialist advice).
Concentration-dependent incompatibility exists with cyclizine, haloperidol and levomepromazine.
Chemical incompatibility with midazolam and glycopyrronium bromide (glycopyrrolate).
Reconstitute powder with water for injection prior to administration.
Olanzapine has a long half-life and there are increasing reports of its safe use when given as a bolus injection.

There is no laboratory physical or chemical stability reported for a reconstituted solution of olanzapine in a syringe driver or a pre-drawn syringe. The reconstituted solution is stable for 1 hour post dilution and therefore its use within a syringe driver should be avoided.
There has been one published report of its use via a 24-hour infusion in the last days of life in a patient already stable on olanzapine.
Reconstitute powder with 2 mL of sodium chloride 0.9%.
Reported administration as bolus dosing or continuous subcutaneous infusion. Due to its long duration of action and half-life, bolus dosing is generally recommended.
Limited compatibility with other medicines; recommendation to administer alone.
Injection site reactions are common, however usually mild.
